title: The Armenian Genocide
subject: histoire
description: Between **1915** and **1916**, the Ottoman government organized the deportation and systematic killing of much of the empire's Armenian population.

hero.hook: The first genocide of the 20th century, nameless for decades, still at the center of a fight over the truth.

blocks.text: Between **1915** and **1916**, in the middle of the First World War, the government of the Ottoman Empire organized the destruction of much of its Armenian population. About **two thirds** of the empire's Armenians died.

This crime, estimated at between **600,000** and **1.5 million** dead, later pushed legal scholars to coin a new word: [[genocide]]. Here is how an ancient minority was branded an enemy within, and then destroyed.

Armenians were one of the oldest Christian populations of Anatolia, the heart of modern Turkey. In the Ottoman Empire, the [[millet]] system left them religious autonomy but an inferior status. In the 19th century the empire declined and nationalism rose. Armenians came to be seen as an internal threat, too close to Russia.

The [[Hamidian massacres]] (**1894-1896**), under Sultan Abdul Hamid II, had already killed **100,000** to **300,000** people. Nobody was punished. In **1908**, the [[Young Turks]], a nationalist movement, raised hopes at first. Then three men, **Enver**, **Talaat**, and **Cemal**, imposed a radical nationalism: an ethnically pure Turkey with no room for non-Muslim minorities.

The world war sped everything up. After the Ottoman defeat at Sarikamish in January 1915, Enver Pasha accused Armenian soldiers of treason. On **April 24, 1915**, in the capital, Constantinople, more than **200** intellectuals and community leaders were arrested and then killed. That date is now the day of commemoration worldwide.

The Polish legal scholar **Raphael Lemkin** had the Armenians explicitly in mind when he later coined the word “genocide.” The UN's [[legal definition of genocide]] (1948) comes straight from that work.

In May, a deportation law gave the expulsions toward the deserts of Mesopotamia a legal frame. The men were often killed just outside their villages. Women, children, and the elderly were driven into forced marches with no food and no protection.

sections.title: Deir ez-Zor and the end of a world

blocks.text: The survivors ended up in makeshift camps in the Syrian desert, above all at **Deir ez-Zor**. In 1916 the last of them were killed there, or died of exhaustion and disease. Neutral diplomats such as the American **Henry Morgenthau** described a “race murder.”

In Anatolia, churches and property were destroyed or seized. Three thousand years of unbroken Armenian life on that land came to an end. After the war the main organizers fled. The new Republic of Turkey turned official forgetting into policy. The survivors formed a vast [[diaspora]], a community scattered across the world.

Even today Turkey admits suffering and massacres in the chaos of war, but rejects the word genocide. Against that official denial, the diaspora campaigns for recognition. France (2001) and the United States (2021), among others, have formally recognized the killings as genocide.

blocks.text: Between **1915** and **1916**, the Ottoman Empire organized the methodical destruction of hundreds of thousands of Armenians. The crime forced the world to invent the word [[genocide]], and its recognition is still a political fight.
